kusala_akusala:
Wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and the “indeterminate dharmas” that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome. The [[three_natures|three natures]] (here the “three natures” mean wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, which share a name with but differ in meaning from the three natures of the imagined / dependent / perfected in [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]]) are the basic framework by which the treatises make value judgments about all dharmas.

The existence of the “indeterminate” is extremely important: it means that not all actions and mental states can be assigned to wholesome or unwholesome — breathing, walking, and unconscious gazing are all indeterminate. Were indeterminate dharmas forcibly drawn into the dichotomy of wholesome and unwholesome, ethical judgment would lose its discriminative power. The treatises therefore further distinguish the “obscured indeterminate” (covered by affliction yet in itself neither wholesome nor unwholesome, such as the innate self-grasping of the manas) from the “unobscured indeterminate”: the former is in itself neither wholesome nor unwholesome **yet is covered by affliction** (such as the innate self-grasping of the manas), while the latter is in itself neither wholesome nor unwholesome **and is not covered by affliction** (such as the ālaya-consciousness, the first five consciousnesses born of karmic maturation, craftsmanship, and deportment). *Cheng Weishi Lun*, fascicle 5, establishes that the criterion for this twofold division lies in “whether it is associated with affliction.”
six_realms:
Gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell beings. These describe the different states of existence brought about by karmic force.

One must note a difference among the schools: the sectarian schools of early Buddhism mostly speak of “five destinies” (nivāsa), that is, without the asuras — asuras are assigned to the destiny of ghosts or to that of the gods; the Mahāyāna mostly speaks of “six realms,” making the asuras a separate destiny. **Asuras** means “non-gods,” referring to those who have the merit of the gods but not the virtue of the gods — because they are given to anger, arrogance, and strife, though they enjoy blessings and pleasures they do not attain the rank of the gods, and so they are made a separate destiny. This difference is often mistaken for a doctrinal disagreement, whereas in fact it is mainly a difference in classificatory habit.

Another point for understanding: the six realms are not six geographical places but primarily “states of existence brought about by karmic force.” The treatises accordingly also say that “a single mind comprises the ten dharma-realms” (Tiantai) — the six realms together with the four noble realms make ten realms, all of which appear in accordance with a single present moment of thought. This reading turns the six realms from cosmology into a theory of mind-nature.
rupa:
Material existence — the four great elements (earth, water, fire, and wind) and the matter derived from them — belonging to the [[conditioned|conditioned dharmas]]; that is, the form aggregate among the five aggregates.

The original sense of “form” (rūpa) is related to “deterioration and resistance”: what deteriorates and has resistance is called form. Modern readers often mistakenly take “form” to mean colour, whereas it is the whole category of the material.

The treatises divide material dharmas into eleven: the five faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body), the five objects (visible form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects), and **unmanifest form** (or form included in the dharma base).

**Unmanifest form** must be discussed separately — it appears to contradict “resistance,” and so *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* fascicle 1 explains it with the verse “In a distracted mind or in a mindless state, it flows along as pure or impure; being of the nature of what the great elements produce — for this reason it is called unmanifest”: a form that is brought about by bodily and verbal karma, is **produced by the great elements** (and so still belongs to form), is **invisible and without resistance** (not seen by the eye and not possessing tangible opposition), and continues in a series, such as the precept-substance obtained upon receiving precepts. The Sarvāstivāda admits this meaning as really existent, while the Sautrāntika and the Yogācāra do not — when reading the various accounts of the precept-substance, one must first discern the standpoint.
six_unconditioned:
Posited by the [[vijnapti_matra|Yogācāra]]: space, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, imperturbability, the cessation of perception and feeling, and [[suchness|suchness]]. Suchness is taken as the perfected nature.

Three of these are held in common with the earlier Sarvāstivāda: the **unconditioned of space** (the nature of non-obstruction, not obstructed by material dharmas), the **unconditioned of analytical cessation** (attained by extinguishing the afflictions through the power of wisdom's discernment), and the **unconditioned of non-analytical cessation** (what is manifested when a dharma does not arise because its causes and conditions are lacking, not through the discernment of wisdom).

Compared with the three unconditioned dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda, the Yogācāra adds three: the unconditioned of imperturbability (attained by extinguishing the feelings of suffering and pleasure from the fourth dhyāna upward), the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling (attained in the attainment of cessation), and the unconditioned of suchness (revealed by the twofold emptiness of all dharmas).

The crucial point is that the Yogācāra includes “suchness” among the unconditioned and takes it as the perfected nature, thereby shifting the centre of gravity of unconditioned dharmas from “cessation” to “suchness” — that is, from “the cessation of what” to “what is manifesting as it really is.” This shift is the watershed between the Yogācāra and the Sarvāstivāda on the question of unconditioned dharmas.
kalpa_cosmology:
The Buddhist scales of time and the extent of the cosmos, the precondition for understanding the claim that “[[samsara|saṃsāra]] is without beginning.”

**Kalpa (Sanskrit *kalpa*)** Traditionally its length is explained by a [[simile_index|simile]]: as with a stone mountain forty li across, brushed once every hundred years with a soft fine cloth — when it is worn away, one kalpa has still not come to an end. A **small kalpa** is reckoned by the increase and decrease of the human lifespan: the human lifespan decreases by one year every hundred years from eighty-four thousand years until it reaches ten years; then it increases by one year every hundred years from ten years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years — this one decrease and one increase make one small kalpa. Twenty small kalpas make one intermediate kalpa, and four intermediate kalpas (formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness) make one great kalpa. One great kalpa comprises the four intermediate kalpas of **formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness** — the world passes through the four periods of formation, duration, destruction, and emptiness, going round and round without beginning or end.

**The three thousand great thousand world system** With Mount Sumeru at the centre, the region illuminated by one sun and moon is one world (one small world); a thousand small worlds make a small thousand world, a thousand small thousand worlds make an intermediate thousand world, and a thousand intermediate thousand worlds make a great thousand world — together called the “three thousand great thousand world system,” the field of conversion of one Buddha. The Sahā world is the field of conversion of Śākyamuni Buddha, while the Land of Bliss is the field of conversion of Amitābha Buddha.

**What this layer is meant to solve** Without these scales of time and space, “saṃsāra” and “sentient beings without bound” would be mere phrases: the number of sentient beings and the length of saṃsāra must exceed any imaginable scale for the bodhisattva path's “liberating all sentient beings” not to be a finite project. And it is precisely because worlds undergo formation and destruction and Buddhas appear and enter nirvāṇa that there is the question of the “continuity of the Buddha-seed” — this is the temporal background of the tathāgatagarbha teaching and the bodhisattva path.
